segments.title: The Fog and the Labyrinth: Opening Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's most labyrinthine novel apart, slowly, with care — and, we hope, with some pleasure.
Bleak House is a novel about fog — literal fog, legal fog, the fog of secrets that settles over families and refuses to lift.
It is also one of the funniest, most heartbreaking, most structurally audacious things the nineteenth century produced.
To help us unpack it, I am joined today by three wonderful readers and thinkers, each of whom brings something quite distinct to the table.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most formidable close readers of Victorian fiction in the country.
He reads novels as moral dramas — stories about character under pressure — and he has no patience for readings that flatten literature into social pamphlet.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what Chancery was, how it worked, and what it did to real people.
He brings the world outside the novel in — the courts, the rookeries, the class machinery — and he can get genuinely angry about all of it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with Bleak House since she was a teenager and has read it more times than she cares to admit.
She cares about the experience of reading — the sentence that makes you stop, re-read, and quietly put the book down for a moment.
We begin, as the novel begins, with atmosphere — with the peculiar world Dickens builds before a single plot has properly started.
James, I want to start with you, because you know Chancery from the inside out — what is Dickens actually doing in these opening pages?
What Dickens is doing is building a satirical monument — and doing it with the confidence of someone who knows the institution is already a ruin.
The Court of Chancery by the 1850s had become a genuine scandal — cases that had run for decades, estates consumed entirely by legal costs.
Dickens captures this perfectly in the long vacation passage.
"The good ships Law and Equity, those teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened, brazen-faced, and not by any means fast-sailing clippers are laid up in ordinary."
That list — teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened, brazen-faced — it mimics the proud language of the commercial shipping trade.
And then the punchline — "not by any means fast-sailing" — arrives with perfect deadpan timing.
The law presents itself with all the grandeur of empire and delivers almost nothing — certainly not speed, certainly not justice.
I would not dispute the satirical force — it is considerable.
But I think what is more interesting is what Dickens does with the image of the Flying Dutchman — the ghostly clients drifting, imploring all they encounter to peruse their papers.
The Gothic enters the legal — and that, I would argue, is not merely satire but genuine moral imagination.
These are souls in purgatory — not because the system is unjust in some abstract institutional sense, but because they have chosen to bind their lives to it.
Dickens is always interested in that — the catastrophe that is freely invited and then cannot be escaped.
And the Gothic is absolutely there from the very first pages of the novel — not just in Chancery but in the Dedlock heritage.
There is this extraordinary backstory — the crippled lady on the terrace at Chesney Wold, day after day, dragging herself up and down with the help of the stone balustrade.
She never complains, never explains — and then one afternoon she drops, and her husband rushes down, and she repulses him.
And she looks at him — the text says fixedly and coldly — and delivers this curse.
"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled."
"And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
That repetition — I will walk, I will walk, I will walk — it has the weight of liturgy.
Dickens earns his Gothic completely here — the Ghost's Walk is not decoration, it is the novel's moral spine.
Caroline is right to hear the liturgical rhythm — that anaphora is not an accident.
But I would press on the word pride — because that is the exact sin that Dickens is tracking through the entire Dedlock story.
Lady Dedlock herself embodies it magnificently — that supreme, icy self-possession.
The curse works not because of any supernatural machinery but because pride is genuinely self-destroying — it carries the calamity within it.
Burke understood that — the great families that fell, fell from within.
Which brings me to the Smallweeds — because if the Dedlocks represent pride destroying itself from above, the Smallweeds represent something corroding from below.
The passage about the Smallweed family tree is one of the most quietly devastating pieces of social description in the novel.
Generation after generation — going out early, marrying late, discarding every form of imaginative life — until something essential is simply gone.
Dickens writes that the house of Smallweed has "discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books, fairy-tales, fictions, and fables."
And the result is described with this extraordinary deadpan precision.

"Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds."
"Gratifying" — the irony in that single word is lethal.
And the image of old monkeys with something depressing on their minds — it is funny and it is horrifying in almost equal measure.
What strikes me about that passage is the specific thing that is listed as banned — story-books, fairy-tales, fictions, fables.
Dickens is doing something almost self-referential there — the Smallweeds have eliminated the very thing the reader is holding in their hands.
No novels — and so no childhood — and so no full humanity.
That connection feels deeply personal to Dickens — and it gives the satire a real sting.
And there is one more moment I want to flag before we move on — because it connects the Gothic of the Ghost's Walk to the novel's present tense.
Later in the novel, Esther is sitting at her favourite spot near Chesney Wold, looking at the Ghost's Walk lying in deep shade — and she is actually picturing the female shape said to haunt it.
And then, out of the wood, through the shadows of the branches, a figure begins to emerge.
"By little and little it revealed itself to be a woman's — a lady's — Lady Dedlock's."
The curse is walking again — except now it is flesh and blood, and the calamity is very close indeed.
The fog, the curse, the family that kills imagination — and Lady Dedlock approaching through the wood.
We have barely started and we are already deep inside the labyrinth.

Coming up, we look more closely at the novel's two narrators — at what it means that Dickens splits his story between the omniscient and Esther Summerson, one of the most unusual first-person voices in all of Victorian fiction.

segments.title: A Man Undone: Richard's Spiral into Obsession

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We turn today to one of the novel's most quietly devastating stories: the ruin of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins as a charming, generous young man, full of possibility — and ends as a wreck consumed by Chancery.
What Dickens shows us, with almost clinical precision, is how that destruction takes root long before it becomes visible.
With me to trace that arc are three readers who know this novel intimately.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings his Oxford-trained eye for moral character — the question of what Richard actually chooses, and why.
Professor James Blackstone situates Richard's predicament in its legal and social reality — what Chancery actually did to real people.
And Caroline Woodcourt reads Richard as the novel asks us to read him — with affection, and with grief.
Let's begin at the beginning of the end — in the chapter where Richard and Ada first declare themselves to Esther, and Mr. Jarndyce speaks to them both with extraordinary tenderness and foresight.
What strikes me every time I re-read this chapter is how happy it is — and how Dickens arranges the happiness so that you already feel its fragility.
Richard and Ada flank Esther on either side, confiding, trusting, almost intoxicated — and Esther's narration just lets them run.
She says — and this is the line that undoes me — she says,
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
There is such warmth in that. Esther laughing at herself, almost, for being as swept up as they are.
But then she pulls them back to earth, and her condition for happiness is quietly devastating: the love must be real, lasting, and inspire constancy, fortitude, and perseverance.
The reader, knowing Richard, knows he will fail every one of those tests.
The chapter is morally rich precisely because Mr. Jarndyce sees all of this — and chooses to believe the best anyway.
He is not naive. His address to Richard is one of the finest pieces of paternal counsel in all of Dickens.
He tells the boy directly, and I think this passage deserves to be heard at full length:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner.
Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
That is not sentiment. That is doctrine — moral doctrine of the most demanding kind.
Jarndyce is telling Richard that love is not a dispensation from effort — it is a demand for it.
Richard will invert this entirely. He will use his love for Ada as a reason to postpone everything else.
And Jarndyce is wise enough to leave a door open — not just for the love, but for its possible dissolution.
The passage where he addresses that possibility is, I think, underrated. He says to them:

"If you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
Now — that is an extraordinary thing for a Victorian guardian figure to say.
He is explicitly refusing the role of the stern patriarch who holds the young to their declarations.
He has no legal power over them — he says so plainly — and he has chosen to make his influence entirely moral.
That is precisely the kind of authority Richard will come to resent and then reject.
And what follows — the moment they leave — Esther's prose simply breaks open.
She watches Richard and Ada pass through a sunlit room, and she gives us this:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness.
So they passed away into the shadow and were gone.
It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
"Passed away into the shadow." In prose about living people. That is what Dickens does.
He writes Richard's eventual death into this moment of joy, so subtly you almost miss it.
The Gothic atmosphere is unmistakable — and I will concede it is doing genuine narrative work there.
But I want to stay with Richard as a character, not a symbol, for a moment.
What we see unfolding across the early chapters is not a young man destroyed by circumstance. It is a young man who consistently chooses ease.
Mrs. Badger's verdict on him — delivered with devastating social precision — is that medicine simply bores him.
He lacks, as she puts it, the positive interest that makes a pursuit one's vocation.
This is not tragedy imposed from without. This is a failure of will — of the very constancy Jarndyce demanded.
Mrs. Badger is a wonderfully sharp observer — far sharper than her social comedy suggests.
She draws the contrast with Woodcourt deliberately — and it is a contrast Dickens means us to feel across the whole novel.
Her exact words are worth hearing:

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
That is precisely the arc Woodcourt follows — and Richard does not.
And here is where the social structure matters: Richard has no vocation, but he does have a lawsuit.
Chancery offers him something medicine and the army never could: a reason to do nothing while believing himself perpetually on the verge of everything.
That's exactly it. Chancery is the perfect psychological fit for Richard's particular weakness.
He doesn't lack ambition — he lacks the capacity to sustain effort through uncertainty and tedium.
And Jarndyce saw that — which is why his counsel is so precise. He tells Richard the world will receive him as he enters it.
What the novel then proceeds to show us, with immense patience, is exactly how Richard enters it — and what the world accordingly gives him back.
A man who mistakes waiting for working — and a legal system perfectly designed to encourage that confusion.
In our next segment, we follow that deterioration further — into what Richard becomes when hope curdled into obsession has nowhere left to go.

segments.title: Secrets and Scaffolding: The Plot of Lady Dedlock

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
Today we're turning our attention to one of the novel's great dramatic engines: the secret life of Lady Dedlock.
Dickens builds her story with extraordinary craft — suspense layered on suspense, identity glimpsed and then withdrawn.
With me, as ever, are Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Ms. Caroline Woodcourt.
I'd like to begin with the mechanism of revelation — the moment Tulkinghorn's net begins to tighten.
What strikes me immediately about Tulkinghorn's message is how it's delivered — not by the lawyer himself, but relayed through Sir Leicester, who hasn't the faintest idea what he's carrying.
Sir Leicester fumbles with his eyeglass, loses his place in the letter, apologises for the delay.
And all the while, Lady Dedlock is waiting — and we are told she looks a little irritated.
That is one of Dickens's most precise psychological observations in this stretch of the novel.
When Tulkinghorn's words finally arrive, they arrive like this — and I'll read them as Sir Leicester does:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Four words at the end. 'I have seen him.' That is the whole trap, sprung in a subordinate clause.
What Dickens understands — and what I think gets overlooked when one reads this novel primarily as a social document — is the moral drama at the heart of that scene.
Lady Dedlock has made a choice, long ago, to bury a life.
And now the consequences of that choice are assembling themselves, patiently, in the hands of a solicitor.
Tulkinghorn is not a villain of circumstance — he is the embodiment of the proposition that secrets have weight, and that weight eventually crushes.
And the passage that follows — the mutual watching — is as fine as anything in the psychological novel.
Dickens writes, and I think one must hear this in full:
"During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another."
'Without any other alteration in their customary deportment.' The armour of manners is never lowered — and that is precisely what makes it so frightening.
Edmund is right that the armour never drops — but I want to stay a moment longer with that extraordinary passage, because it doesn't stop there.
Dickens keeps pressing inward, into what cannot be seen, what neither character will ever admit.
He asks — and I find this almost unbearably tense to read aloud:

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
'All this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.' That phrase — 'for the time' — is devastating.
It tells us, with the quietest possible certainty, that it will not remain hidden.
That 'for the time' does enormous work, doesn't it — the whole novel compressed into a subordinating clause.
Now, the secret doesn't only have consequences for the adults who hold it — it ripples forward into Esther Summerson's life.
Caroline, you've written about the weight of guilt imposed on children in this novel — what do we make of the letter described in Chapter Seventeen?
That passage from Chapter Seventeen is one that stops me every time, because the cruelty it describes is so completely sincere.
Jarndyce is explaining to Esther the spirit in which the letter about her childhood was written — and the phrase he uses is simply damning.
He speaks of:
"the distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was quite innocent."
'Quite innocent.' Not merely innocent — quite innocent. The adverb is Dickens insisting that we feel the full obscenity of the proposition.
And what Jarndyce says next — that he 'felt concerned for the little creature, in her darkened life' — that tenderness, after the harshness, is almost too much to bear.
Caroline's instinct about the adverb is precisely right, and I would add only this: that 'distorted religion' is one of Dickens's most carefully chosen phrases in the whole novel.
He does not say false religion. He does not say hypocrisy.
He says distorted — which implies something that was once coherent, and has been bent out of shape by guilt and self-punishment into something monstrous.
The godmother is not a villain of cold calculation in the Tulkinghorn mould — she is a woman destroyed by shame.
And Dickens insists we hold both truths at once: that Esther suffered terribly, and that the suffering came from a broken love.
There is something historically precise in that phrase 'distorted religion' as well, which is worth naming.
The evangelical tradition in early Victorian England had a very specific theology of shame — of the sins of the parent visited upon the child — that Dickens is clearly drawing on here.
It wasn't a fringe belief. It was respectable. Taught from pulpits.
Dickens is writing for an audience that would recognise that framework — and would know exactly what kind of household Esther had grown up in.
That context makes Jarndyce's response — his simple human concern for 'the little creature' — feel like an act of genuine moral resistance, not sentimentality.
And all of that history — the shame, the expiation, the 'darkened life' — is what Esther carries with her, unknowingly, when she first encounters Lady Dedlock.
Which brings us to what I consider one of the most uncanny moments in all of Dickens — the recognition scene in Chapter Eighteen.
Caroline — this passage is very much in your territory.
It is my territory — I've read it probably thirty times, and it still gives me a kind of chill.
Esther sees Lady Dedlock for the first time, having never met her.
And something in her stirs that she cannot name or account for — not a memory, but something older than memory.
Dickens's rendering of it is extraordinarily delicate:

"And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."
'Stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll.' That image — that solitary, tender image of a child attending to her doll before herself — it undoes me completely.
And yet Dickens is careful — meticulously careful — to have Esther insist she has never seen this woman before.
'Although I had never seen this lady's face before in all my life — I was quite sure of it — absolutely certain.'
The triple insistence — 'never seen,' 'quite sure,' 'absolutely certain' — is Dickens making sure we understand that this is not ordinary recognition.
What Esther is experiencing is something biology knows before the conscious mind does.
James is right that the recognition is pre-rational — but I would frame it slightly differently.
Dickens is dramatising something that moral philosophers have long struggled with: the way identity is not purely self-constructed, but received — inherited — whether we will it or not.
And the passage that follows is, I think, where Dickens achieves something close to the sublime.

"And yet I—I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady, whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour."
'Seemed to arise before my own eyes.' She becomes, for a moment, visible to herself — a self she had not known to look for.
That is not a social observation. That is pure novelistic metaphysics.
And the phrase 'on whose birthday there was no rejoicing' — Dickens slips that in as if it were merely a description, and it is a stab through the heart.
Esther has been so thoroughly taught that her existence is shameful that she has internalised it as simple fact.
And now, here in a fashionable room, a woman she has never met is — without knowing it — summoning that child back into existence.
There is also this: Esther explicitly considers whether the resemblance is to her godmother — and rejects it.
The expression is entirely different — 'the stern decision which had worn into my godmother's face, like weather into rocks' is absent from Lady Dedlock entirely.
What Esther feels is not resemblance — it is something underneath resemblance. The blood recognising blood.
'The blood recognising blood' — that's beautifully put.
What Dickens has engineered — across these chapters — is a kind of dramatic irony of the body: Esther knows everything except what she knows.
And Tulkinghorn, meanwhile, is quietly assembling the same knowledge from the other direction.
Two people converging on the same secret — one with dread, one with relish.
We'll pick up the consequences of that convergence in our next segment.

segments.title: The Crossing-Sweep's Requiem: Jo and Social Cruelty

utterances.text: We turn now to one of the novel's most devastating sequences — the inquest into the death of Nemo, and what it reveals about a boy named Jo.
Jo is a crossing-sweeper — a child who lives in the streets, sweeps mud from the crossing for halfpenny tips, and knows almost nothing of the world except its cruelty.
Caroline, I want to start with you, because I know these passages hit you hard as a reader.
They do — and they hit hard precisely because Dickens refuses to soften them.
The moment Jo appears before the inquest — to give testimony — Dickens gives us this extraordinary catalogue of negatives.
Listen to how it sounds when you read it aloud:
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Four words, then three words. The sentences get shorter as the deprivation deepens.
Dickens could have given us a paragraph of misery — instead he gives us a list, and the list is the misery.
And then — just when you think it cannot get any bleaker — comes the question: "What's home?"
What the passage also records — with extraordinary precision — is the legal mechanism of exclusion.
Jo cannot testify. He is disqualified as a witness because he cannot demonstrate knowledge of an oath.
Now, that was not a fictional invention — that was the actual law of evidence operating in England at mid-century.
A child too uneducated to understand religious obligation could not speak in a court of law — however truthful, however present, however directly relevant his evidence.
And the bitter irony is that Jo tells us himself he knows it's wicked to tell a lie — and that he'll tell the truth.
The law constructs a category of person whose moral integrity is simply invisible to it.
James is quite right about the legal architecture — but I'd want to resist reducing this passage to a pamphlet.
What strikes me most is the grammar of the passage — the relentless third person, the stunted syntax mimicking Jo's own arrested development.
Dickens is not merely reporting Jo's deprivation; he is enacting it in the very form of his prose.
And then, later, there is a moment of extraordinary tenderness — when Jo comes at night to the gate of the graveyard.
The prose describes him — and I want to emphasise this — not as a boy, but as a figure, as an "it."
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
"It" — not he. The dehumanisation is Dickens's own, and it is deliberate, and it is devastating.
Society has rendered Jo so marginal that even the narrator momentarily cannot bring himself to say "he."
Edmund, that observation about "it" — I've read this passage a dozen times and it still stops me cold each time.
Because the action is so tender — the quiet sweeping, the careful tidying of a step that nobody else tends — and the pronoun is so brutally impersonal.
And then Dickens shifts register entirely — and addresses Jo directly, in the second person.
He writes — and this is the passage I keep returning to:
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
That little embedded quote — "He wos wery good to me" — in Jo's own phonetic voice, inside the narrator's address.
It is the most heartbreaking sentence in the chapter. Possibly in the book.
And notice what that loyalty is attached to — a dead man about whom the entire neighbourhood has spread vicious rumour.
Mrs. Piper's testimony is played for comedy — Dickens is very funny about her, undeniably — but the content is sinister.
Dickens gives us Mrs. Piper's testimony as a cascade of rumour, hearsay, and unanchored fear — with almost no punctuation to slow it down.
"the plaintive — so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased — was reported to have sold himself."
"Sold himself" — meaning sold his soul to the devil. That is the neighbourhood's verdict on a man they barely knew.
And this gossip, this tangle of prejudice and mispronunciation, is what passes for community knowledge in a Victorian slum court.
Against all of that, Jo's four words — "He wos wery good to me" — stand as a kind of incorruptible testimony.
And that is where Dickens locates grace — not in the institutions, not in the law, not in the community's moral consensus, but in that single act of gratitude.
The narrator says Jo is not quite in outer darkness — and the phrasing is deliberately theological.
"A distant ray of light" — it is not redemption, it is not salvation, it is something far more fragile and far more honest than that.
It is the capacity to recognise kindness received — and to be faithful to it, even in the dark, even at a locked iron gate.
What's remarkable is that Dickens extends that faithfulness to Jo even as the novel — and the law — and the neighbours — all conspire to render him invisible.
The narrator sees him. The reader sees him. And the novel insists that that act of seeing is itself a moral obligation.
We'll return shortly to the wider world of Bleak House — the fog that opens the novel, and the institution that Dickens holds most responsible for it.

segments.title: Laughter in the Machinery: Dickens's Comic Vision

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel apart sentence by sentence to find out what makes it tick.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring something that tends to get overlooked in serious discussions of this novel — its comedy.
Bleak House is a novel about suffering, injustice, and institutional rot — and yet it is also one of the funniest books in the English language.
To help us think about how those two things coexist, I'm joined by three wonderful guests.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been the moral imagination of the Victorian novel — he'll keep us honest about character and craft.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows precisely what the institutions Dickens lampoons actually were — and what they cost ordinary people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and has an unerring ear for when Dickens's prose is doing something extraordinary.
Let's begin with Lawrence Boythorn — surely one of the great comic creations in English fiction.
Boythorn is a delight — genuinely one of those characters you read aloud to anyone who happens to be nearby.
What Dickens gives him is this magnificent escalating rhythm — each outrage bigger than the last, each retaliation more absurd.
He describes his dispute with Sir Leicester over a right of way as though narrating a small war.
There's the moment he deploys a fire engine against Sir Leicester's workman — and then the gate gets chopped down and burned.
And then it arrives at this perfect couplet of belligerent logic — listen to the rhythm of it.
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
That final "Ha, ha, ha" is pure Dickens — triumphant, unrepentant, completely delighted with itself.
What strikes me about Boythorn is that the comedy is inseparable from his goodness.
He is preposterous — utterly, magnificently preposterous — but never mean.
His fury at Sir Leicester is comic precisely because it carries no malice — it is a fury of principle, almost innocent in its exuberance.
Dickens understood something that Johnson grasped too: that the truly comic character is always a little larger than life, never diminished by the joke.
Boythorn calls Sir Leicester, among other things, "the most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull" — and yet we leave the scene admiring Boythorn, not merely laughing at him.
There is a legal dimension here that sharpens the comedy considerably.
Rights of way disputes in the nineteenth century were genuinely savage affairs — they consumed fortunes and reputations in the courts.
What Dickens perceives is that the law doesn't resolve the dispute — it simply gives both parties a formal vocabulary for continuing to fight.
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass" — that isn't just a joke; it is a precise description of how litigation actually worked.
Two men of means circling each other in perpetuity, the courts enriching themselves handsomely on the friction.
James's point about perpetuity connects to something larger in the novel — the Boodle and Noodle passage does exactly the same thing with government.
The political class is caught in the same endless loop — not litigation, but patronage.
Lord Boodle explains to Sir Leicester with perfect gravity that the country faces catastrophe.
"What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces (as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock) because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The comedy is in that parenthesis — "as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock" — Dickens slipping the knife in mid-sentence.
I confess the Boodle-Noodle passage has always struck me as Dickens at his most dangerously schematic.
The accumulation of rhyming names — Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, Goodle, Hoodle — is a genuine comic device, but it risks reducing human beings to cyphers.
One wonders what Burke would have made of it — the argument that governance is merely the distribution of sinecures is compelling as satire, but is it the whole truth?
And yet — and I say this reluctantly — the laughter it produces is genuine, because we recognise something real in it.
I'm afraid I can't follow Edmund into that reluctance — for me the Noodle passage is almost documentary.
The distribution of offices in early Victorian government was precisely that system — cabinet posts assigned to manage personal and factional loyalties, not competence.
The joke is that Lord Boodle presents this as a constitutional crisis, when it is merely a question of whether a mediocrity can be comfortably placed.
Dickens makes it absurd by piling up the names, but the underlying machinery was entirely real.
I want to bring in another kind of comedy — darker, stranger — because Dickens isn't only doing the big set-piece laughs.
The beadle scene — the inquest witnesses — is almost surreal in its catalogue of institutional uselessness.
The beadle goes about seeking anyone who can give evidence, and Dickens tells us he is
"immediately referred to innumerable people who can tell nothing whatever."
It's funny — but it is also the machinery by which a death goes uninvestigated.
And then there's the policeman — unmoved, lounging, beating his white gloves together, stopping now and then "to look casually about for anything between a lost child and a murder."
The comedy and the indictment are the same gesture.
That is well observed — and it speaks to something I find most admirable in Dickens at his best.
The comedy never lets the reader off the moral hook.
You laugh at the beadle's imbecility, but Dickens has arranged matters so that your laughter is itself implicated in the system's indifference.
That is a considerably more sophisticated trick than simple satire.
The beadle was a real office — a parish functionary whose authority was largely ceremonial and frequently ridiculous.
Dickens's contemporaries would have recognised the type immediately — someone invested with a little brief authority and completely incapable of exercising it usefully.
The boy who gets arrested for singing — and released on condition he simply moves along — is the comic punctuation, but it's also showing us how law actually operated at street level.
Discretionary, theatrical, concerned above all with not being embarrassed.
There's one more passage I can't let us leave without — the ending of the Snagsby chapter.
It's funny in a way that slowly turns gothic as you read it.
Mrs. Snagsby has become convinced her husband is hiding something — and from this chapter forward she becomes his shadow, literally and figuratively.
The writing is almost incantatory — you need to hear it whole.
"And henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."

"And into whatsoever atmosphere of secrecy his own shadow may pass, let all concerned in the secrecy beware! For the watchful Mrs. Snagsby is there too—bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow."
"Bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh" — that's the marriage service, turned into a surveillance notice.
That is, I think, the most compressed example in the novel of how Dickens's comedy works at its deepest level.
The joke about Mrs. Snagsby's jealous surveillance is perfectly comic — and simultaneously it inverts every sacred formula of marriage.
The comedy is the vehicle for something quite cold.
And it's worth noting that Mrs. Snagsby's paranoia, absurd as it is, isn't entirely wrong — there are secrets being kept.
Dickens makes her the comic figure, but the comedy is layered over something genuinely murky.
The beadle, the politicians, the warring baronets, the suspicious wife — they are all comic expressions of a world in which information, authority, and secrecy are being constantly mishandled.
What emerges from all of this — Boythorn's war, the Noodle parliament, the beadle's magnificent uselessness, and Mrs. Snagsby stalking the shadows — is a very particular kind of laughter.
It's laughter that doesn't quite release you — it implicates you even as it delights you.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the novel's great darkness — what Bleak House looks like when the comedy stops.

segments.title: Entanglement and Irony: How Bleak House Holds Its Threads

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's great novel apart — carefully — and try to understand how it holds together.
I'm joined today by three readers who know this book with a depth and seriousness it fully deserves.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose faith in the moral imagination of great fiction is, to put it mildly, unshakeable.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who reminds us that the institutions Dickens depicts were lethally real — not merely theatrical backdrops.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House more times than she might wish to admit, and brings to it an ear for every note Dickens strikes.
Today we're looking at one of the novel's central tragedies in miniature: the slow entanglement of Richard Carstone in the Chancery suit.
Dickens shows us this deterioration through Esther's eyes — with extraordinary irony and a very quiet kind of heartbreak.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because Richard is, I think, a character you feel rather strongly about.
Strongly is one word for it.
Richard Carstone is one of those characters who breaks your heart precisely because Dickens lets you watch the breaking in real time.
What strikes me every time I return to chapter seventeen is how Dickens uses Richard's own voice against him — with tremendous gentleness.
He gives Richard this moment of almost painful self-awareness, where Richard actually diagnoses his own condition.
The passage reads — and I find this almost unbearable —

"I don't know how it is; I seem to want something or other to stand by. Even you have no idea how fond I am of Ada (my darling cousin, I love you, so much!), but I don't settle down to constancy in other things. It's such uphill work, and it takes such a time!"
That parenthesis — "my darling cousin, I love you, so much!" — is devastating, because it is entirely sincere.
He genuinely loves Ada. And he genuinely cannot hold to anything. Both things are completely true.
Caroline is right to single out that parenthesis. It is the rhetorical signature of the whole character.
Richard Carstone is not a villain, nor even — in the conventional sense — a weakling. He is a young man of genuine feeling and no moral traction.
The distinction matters enormously. Johnson would have said he lacks the capacity for self-command — not the desire for it.
What Esther does, in chapter seventeen, is apply moral pressure with extraordinary tact.
She tells us that she hinted to Richard that his carelessness of himself might shade into carelessness of Ada —
"it was a part of his affectionate consideration for her not to slight the importance of a step that might influence both their lives."
The phrase "affectionate consideration" is doing very precise work. Esther is not appealing to Richard's will — she knows his will is unreliable.
She appeals instead to his love. And love, for the moment, makes him almost grave.
I want to come at this from a different angle, because there is something historically precise happening in Richard's self-diagnosis that I think we risk sentimentalising.
When Richard says he wants to enter Kenge's office to study law, Dickens shows us exactly what kind of studying he intends.
The passage is quite nakedly revealing:
"If I went into Kenge's office...I should have my eye on the—hum!—the forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it."
That "hum!" — that tiny hesitation — is Dickens at his most precise. Richard knows he is saying something he shouldn't.
He calls Chancery "the forbidden ground" — which is Jarndyce's language, a prohibition he has internalised just enough to feel sheepish about transgressing.

The real Chancery, I should say, was precisely this kind of trap — a jurisdiction that kept people tethered to litigation for decades, spending every resource on the process of waiting for a resolution that never came.
Richard's instinct to keep his eye on it is understandable. It is also exactly how the machinery caught you.
James, that word "machinery" is exactly right — and it leads me to a passage later in the novel, in chapter twenty-three, that I find almost impossible to read without feeling the trap closing.
Esther is watching Richard's visits to Chancery become habitual, watching him befriend Miss Flite, watching him build his delusive certainty that a favourable judgment is imminent.
And then Dickens gives us this sentence — and I think it is one of the great sentences in the novel:
"what a fatal link was riveting between his fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind."
The parallelism is devastating. Fresh against faded. Free against caged. Youth against age.
And Esther sees it. But Richard never does. That asymmetry of vision is the whole tragedy.

What Caroline has just described is, I think, the particular genius of Esther as narrator — and I say this as someone who has heard Esther accused of being too meek, too modest, too self-deprecating to carry a novel.
The accusation misses the point entirely. Esther sees with perfect clarity. She sees what others cannot or will not see.
The passage about Jarndyce in chapter seventeen is a case in point. Esther notices something that changes everything:
"This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with something of a shadow on their benevolent expression."
A shadow on a benevolent expression. That is a very small thing to observe. And a very large thing to report.
Jarndyce's feelings for Ada and Richard are complex — more complex, perhaps, than even he would admit to himself. Esther registers that complexity in a single glance.
This is not a meek narrator. This is a narrator of the most penetrating moral intelligence.

Edmund has put his finger on something I want to extend slightly, because the shadow on Jarndyce's expression is not merely personal — it opens onto the whole structure of guardianship as a legal and social institution.
Richard and Ada are wards of court. They exist within Chancery's jurisdiction in a very particular way.
Jarndyce has positioned himself as their protector against Chancery — and yet the suit that threatens to consume Richard is the same suit from which Jarndyce himself benefits.
Esther describes Richard's industry as "all misdirected" — and she is right, in the moral sense. But in the legal sense, Richard's instinct is not entirely irrational.
Chancery suits did sometimes resolve. Estates did occasionally distribute. What the court offered was the structure of legitimate expectation — which is exactly what makes it so effective as a trap.
Richard's delusion is not simply a character flaw. It is the precise product of the system he inhabits. That is what makes Dickens's indictment so powerful — and so uncomfortable.
I would not dispute James's account of the machinery. But I am always a little wary of readings that absolve the individual entirely by pointing to the system.
Dickens is not writing a sociological treatise. He is writing a novel — which means the moral fate of individuals matters independently of their circumstances.
Richard knows what he is doing. That "hum!" James mentioned — that hesitation before "the forbidden ground" — is not innocence. It is a small, telling failure of will.
And Dickens shows us this accumulation of small failures — each one confirming the pattern — until the pattern becomes destiny.
That is how tragedy works — not through one catastrophic decision but through the slow accrual of what one allows oneself to become.
I think Edmund and James are both right — and what's remarkable is that Dickens seems to intend precisely that double vision.
Richard is simultaneously a victim of a corrupt system and a young man who fails to resist it — and Esther, who loves him, holds both truths at once.
There is a heartbreaking phrase in chapter twenty-three — Esther calls him "my poor, dear, sanguine Richard" — and the word "sanguine" carries all the irony.
Sanguine means hopeful, confident — but it also meant, in its older sense, ruled by the blood. Driven by temperament rather than reason.
Dickens loads that single word with the system's indictment and Esther's tenderness at the same time. That's the verbal music I keep coming back to.
That double vision — the system's indictment and Esther's tenderness held in a single word — feels like the key to why these passages stay with readers long after the plot has faded.
Richard Carstone as both culpable and ensnared, Jarndyce watched with a newly shadowed eye, Miss Flite's caged birds casting their long, ominous shadow forward.
The threads of this novel do not merely connect — they tighten.
We'll continue after the break, where we'll be turning to the fog — that famous, omnipresent fog — and asking what Dickens really wants it to do.

segments.title: The Web Tightens: Convergence and Reckoning

utterances.text: We've arrived at the closing chapter of today's episode, and fittingly, we're ending where Bleak House itself seems most to breathe — in suspense.
The passages before us concern secrets — kept, suspected, and almost unbearably felt.
Lady Dedlock's hidden past is drawing tighter around her, and Dickens is orchestrating the pressure with extraordinary craft.
Edmund, I want to begin with you — because the scenes between Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn are, I think, among the most psychologically charged in the novel.
They are, and I think the key to understanding those scenes is that both combatants are, in their very different ways, supremely accomplished performers.
Dickens gives us the surface — the dinner table, the drawing room — and then he gives us what lies beneath, and refuses to let either plane dissolve into the other.
The passage describing their repeated encounters is, I would say, a masterpiece of what one might call sustained dramatic irony.
Dickens writes — and I must read this in full, because the architecture of the sentence earns every word —
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
"Mr. Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
Notice that the word 'always' governs both portraits — and it is a quietly terrible word in this context.
It suggests not routine, but compulsion — two people locked in a performance neither can escape.
That word 'always' — yes, Edmund, exactly.
But what strikes me even more is what comes at the end of that passage — the turn inward, into what cannot be shown.
Dickens writes — and this is where the prose becomes almost unbearable —

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares;"
"what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
That phrase — 'for the time' — is doing extraordinary work.
It tells us this concealment has a term, that revelation is already approaching, even as we watch the masks stay perfectly in place.
I want to hold onto that image of Tulkinghorn as 'speechless repository of noble confidences' for a moment.
Because what Dickens is capturing, with alarming precision, is a real feature of Victorian professional life.
The family solicitor was not merely a legal technician — he was the keeper of everything a great household could not afford to have spoken aloud.
Tulkinghorn's power is precisely that he knows where the bodies are buried — sometimes almost literally.
And yet his relationship with Lady Dedlock is not simply blackmail — or not yet.
It is something colder and more institutional — a lawyer managing a liability on behalf of a family who doesn't yet know they have one.
James, I'd push back very gently on framing this purely institutionally.
Tulkinghorn is not merely a professional type — he has, one senses, a genuine animus toward Lady Dedlock.
There is something in her aristocratic disdain that has affronted him — and he means to bring her down, not simply to manage her.
Which is, of course, the moral tragedy at the centre of the book — that a man of low passion is given the power of a great institution.
And into this world of managed secrets comes Esther herself — who we now know has been the object of precisely such careful concealment.
Caroline, the passages from Chapter Seventeen — Jarndyce's account of the letter, and what it reveals about Esther's origins — how do those land for you as a reader?
They're devastating, and deliberately so.
Dickens is asking Esther — and us — to hear, at second hand, the language in which her own existence was described by her mother.
Jarndyce reads from the letter — and notice how Dickens keeps that letter at one remove, reported rather than directly quoted.
He says — and I find this almost unbearable to read —
"It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years old, in some such cruel words as those which live in your remembrance."
'Cruel words' — not harsh, not blunt, but cruel.
Esther already carries those words inside her, and now she learns that they came, ultimately, from her own mother.
What Jarndyce's account also reveals, historically, is just how much legal and social infrastructure was required to erase a child.
The passage tells us — in Jarndyce's own words —
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
That phrase — 'for any human consideration' — is a phrase with real legal weight.
It means she has been asked — by Kenge, presumably — and has refused absolutely.
In Victorian law, an illegitimate child had essentially no claim on its mother — and a mother who chose silence was legally unreachable.
Lady Dedlock is not simply choosing shame — she is working within a system that makes her choice invisible, and therefore invulnerable.
I think we should be careful, though, not to reduce Lady Dedlock to a social case study.
What strikes me about Jarndyce's account is the phrase 'stern passion and power' — this is not a woman defeated by convention.
She acts — she writes the letter, she arranges the provision — under an internal compulsion that Dickens regards with something very close to reverence.
The letter was written, Jarndyce tells us —
"with a stern passion and power that rendered it unlike all other letters I have ever read."
Dickens is telling us that this woman's inner life is exceptional — and that her tragedy is proportionate to that exceptionalism.
And then comes the moment when Esther and Lady Dedlock meet — and something passes between them that neither woman can name.
Caroline, this is your passage — and I suspect you've read it many times.
Many times — and it never loses its force.
What Dickens does here is give it to Esther to narrate — this woman who has been denied her own history is the one who records the moment of recognition.
And the prose lifts into something almost Shakespearean —
"Shall I ever forget the rapid beating at my heart, occasioned by the look I met as I stood up!"
"Shall I ever forget the manner in which those handsome proud eyes seemed to spring out of their languor and to hold mine!"
That rhetorical repetition — 'Shall I ever forget' — is not Esther's usual register.
Something is pressing through the prose — something too large for her habitual modesty to contain.
What I find striking is the physical precision of it — 'spring out of their languor.'
Lady Dedlock's entire social armour is built on that languor — the exhausted deity, as we've heard.
In one involuntary glance, it fails her — and Esther sees it fail.
Dickens gives us the great secret as a bodily event — the eyes give it away before the mind can suppress it.
And yet Dickens writes — with that saving qualification — 'It was only a moment before I cast mine down — released again, if I may say so — on my book.'
That parenthesis — 'if I may say so' — is vintage Esther.
She retreats from the enormity of what she's experienced into characteristic self-doubt — and in doing so, she reveals just how enormous it was.
The novel is doing what only the greatest novels do — making the unspeakable visible through the very act of not quite saying it.
Edmund, James, Caroline — that feels like exactly the right place to end.
A glance that lasts a moment, a letter written in stern passion, a solicitor who 'knows' without ever saying — Dickens builds his web one concealment at a time.
Thank you all for your company today on Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll be back next time with more of this extraordinary novel — which, as today's discussion has shown, never stops rewarding a second, or a twentieth, look.

c19:p0.text:
It is the long vacation in the regions of Chancery Lane. The good
ships Law and Equity, those teak-built, copper-bottomed,
iron-fastened, brazen-faced, and not by any means fast-sailing
clippers are laid up in ordinary. The Flying Dutchman, with a crew of
ghostly clients imploring all whom they may encounter to peruse their
papers, has drifted, for the time being, heaven knows where. The
courts are all shut up; the public offices lie in a hot sleep.
Westminster Hall itself is a shady solitude where nightingales might
sing, and a tenderer class of suitors than is usually found there,
walk.
c19:p0.summary: During the long vacation, the legal profession is dormant; the courts, offices, and Westminster Hall are empty as lawyers and clerks scatter across the continent.
c19:p0.best_quote: The good ships Law and Equity, those teak-built, copper-bottomed, iron-fastened, brazen-faced, and not by any means fast-sailing clippers are laid up in ordinary.

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.
c7:p59.best_quote: I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!

c21:p4.text:
His spirit shone through his son, to whom he had always preached of
“going out” early in life and whom he made a clerk in a sharp
scrivener’s office at twelve years old. There the young gentleman
improved his mind, which was of a lean and anxious character, and
developing the family gifts, gradually elevated himself into the
discounting profession. Going out early in life and marrying late, as
his father had done before him, he too begat a lean and
anxious-minded son, who in his turn, going out early in life and
marrying late, became the father of Bartholomew and Judith Smallweed,
twins. During the whole time consumed in the slow growth of this
family tree, the house of Smallweed, always early to go out and late
to marry, has strengthened itself in its practical character, has
discarded all amusements, discountenanced all story-books,
fairy-tales, fictions, and fables, and banished all levities
whatsoever. Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born
to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced
have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something
depressing on their minds.
c21:p4.summary: The narrator traces how successive Smallweed generations have perpetuated a culture of early entry into commerce and late marriage, deliberately eliminating all levity and amusement, producing stunted premature adults.
c21:p4.best_quote: Hence the gratifying fact that it has had no child born to it and that the complete little men and women whom it has produced have been observed to bear a likeness to old monkeys with something depressing on their minds.

c36:p18.text:
I was resting at my favourite point after a long ramble, and Charley
was gathering violets at a little distance from me. I had been
looking at the Ghost’s Walk lying in a deep shade of masonry afar off
and picturing to myself the female shape that was said to haunt it
when I became aware of a figure approaching through the wood. The
perspective was so long and so darkened by leaves, and the shadows of
the branches on the ground made it so much more intricate to the eye,
that at first I could not discern what figure it was. By little and
little it revealed itself to be a woman’s—a lady’s—Lady Dedlock’s.
She was alone and coming to where I sat with a much quicker step, I
observed to my surprise, than was usual with her.
c36:p18.summary: As Esther rests at her favorite spot, a woman emerges through the wood—Lady Dedlock, approaching with unusual haste and emotion.

c13:p99.text:
There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.
c13:p99.summary: Richard and Ada confide to Esther their mutual love, placing themselves on either side of her. Esther counsels them about the demands of enduring love and promises to speak to Mr. Jarndyce.
c13:p99.best_quote: They went on in their own wild way for a little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake.

c13:p113.text:
“Rick,” said Mr. Jarndyce, “I am glad to have won your confidence. I
hope to preserve it. When I contemplated these relations between us
four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new
interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the
possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don’t be shy, Ada,
don’t be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together.
I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was
afar off, Rick, afar off!”
c13:p113.summary: Mr. Jarndyce addresses Richard and Ada, confirming he is glad to have their confidence and that he did contemplate their union as a possibility.
c13:p113.best_quote: When I contemplated these relations between us four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together. I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”
c13:p118.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.
c13:p118.best_quote: Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it.

c13:p115.text:
“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”
c13:p115.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.
c13:p115.best_quote: I will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me, Rick!)—don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it.

c13:p124.text:
The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up
in his face, listening, and seemed to see nothing else. So young, so
beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through
the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the
years to come and making them all years of brightness. So they passed
away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that
had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun
was clouded over.
c13:p124.summary: As Ada and Richard leave, Esther observes them passing through sunlit rooms, young and full of hope, but the sun clouds over as they depart, suggesting a foreboding shadow.

So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over.

“My dear Miss Summerson,” she replied, “on Mr. Carstone’s character
and conduct. He is of such a very easy disposition that probably he
would never think it worth while to mention how he really feels, but
he feels languid about the profession. He has not that positive
interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided
impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a
tiresome pursuit. Now, this is not promising. Young men like Mr.
Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can

c12:p11.text:
“He sends—I really beg your pardon—he sends,” says Sir Leicester,
selecting the letter and unfolding it, “a message to you. Our
stopping to change horses as I came to his postscript drove it out of
my memory. I beg you’ll excuse me. He
 says—”  Sir Leicester is so
long in taking out his eye-glass and adjusting it that my Lady looks
a little irritated. “He says ‘In the matter of the right of way—’ I
beg your pardon, that’s not the place. He says—yes! Here I have it!
He says, ‘I beg my respectful compliments to my Lady, who, I hope,
has benefited by the change. Will you do me the favour to mention (as
it may interest her) that I have something to tell her on her return
in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery
suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen
him.’”
c12:p11.summary: Sir Leicester slowly reads Mr. Tulkinghorn's message stating that he has discovered the identity and location of the man who copied the affidavit Lady Dedlock inquired about.

During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady

“Your early recollection, my dear, will supply the gloomy medium

And, very strangely, there was something quickened within me,
associated with the lonely days at my godmother’s; yes, away even to
the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little
glass after dressing my doll. And this, although I had never seen

c18:p44.text:
I felt it to be an unmeaning weakness in me and tried to overcome it
by attending to the words I heard. Then, very strangely, I seemed to
hear them, not in the reader’s voice, but in the well-remembered
voice of my godmother. This made me think, did Lady Dedlock’s face
accidentally resemble my godmother’s? It might be that it did, a
little; but the expression was so different, and the stern decision
which had worn into my godmother’s face, like weather into rocks, was
so completely wanting in the face before me that it could not be that
resemblance which had struck me. Neither did I know the loftiness and
haughtiness of Lady Dedlock’s face, at all, in any one. And yet I—I,
little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on
whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own
eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady,
whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I
perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour.

c11:p78.text:
Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don’t know that everybody
has two names. Never heerd of sich a think. Don’t know that Jo is
short for a longer name. Thinks it long enough for HIM. HE don’t find
no fault with it. Spell it? No. HE can’t spell it. No father, no
mother, no friends. Never been to school. What’s home? Knows a
broom’s a broom, and knows it’s wicked to tell a lie. Don’t recollect
who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both. Can’t
exactly say what’ll be done to him arter he’s dead if he tells a lie
to the gentlemen here, but believes it’ll be something wery bad to
punish him, and serve him right—and so he’ll tell the truth.

c11:p98.text:
With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to
the outside of the iron gate. It holds the gate with its hands and
looks in between the bars, stands looking in for a little while.
c11:p98.summary: A slouching figure (Jo) comes through the tunnel-court to the cemetery gate and looks in.

c11:p99.text:
It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and

c11:p100.text:
Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness, who “can’t
exactly say” what will be done to him in greater hands than men’s,
thou art not quite in outer darkness. There is something like a
distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: “He wos wery

c11:p74.text:

c9:p49.text:
“By my soul,” exclaimed Mr. Boythorn, suddenly firing another volley,
“that fellow is, and his father was, and his grandfather was, the
most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by
some inexplicable mistake of Nature, born in any station of life but
a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should
not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and
living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the
existence of those lurking ruffians. He brings actions for trespass;
I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and
battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha,
ha!”
c9:p49.summary: Boythorn launches an elaborate account of his escalating disputes with Sir Leicester over a right of way, detailing the volleys of letters, his theatrical retaliation with a fire engine, his destruction of gates, and the counter-actions in law, all recounted with relish and concluding with triumphant laughter.
c9:p49.best_quote: He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!

c12:p56.text:
Then there is my Lord Boodle, of considerable reputation with his
party, who has known what office is and who tells Sir Leicester
Dedlock with much gravity, after dinner, that he really does not see
to what the present age is tending. A debate is not what a debate
used to be; the House is not what the House used to be; even a
Cabinet is not what it formerly was. He perceives with astonishment
that supposing the present government to be overthrown, the limited
choice of the Crown, in the formation of a new ministry, would lie
between Lord Coodle and Sir Thomas Doodle—supposing it to be
impossible for the Duke of Foodle to act with Goodle, which may be
assumed to be the case in consequence of the breach arising out of
that affair with Hoodle. Then, giving the Home Department and the
leadership of the House of Commons to Joodle, the Exchequer to
Koodle, the Colonies to Loodle, and the Foreign Office to Moodle,
what are you to do with Noodle? You can’t offer him the Presidency of
the Council; that is reserved for Poodle. You can’t put him in the
Woods and Forests; that is hardly good enough for Quoodle. What
follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces
(as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock)
because you can’t provide for Noodle!
c12:p56.summary: Lord Boodle explains to Sir Leicester that government is failing because there is no office suitable for Noodle after all the important positions are distributed among his equally mediocre associates.
c12:p56.best_quote: What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces (as is made manifest to the patriotism of Sir Leicester Dedlock) because you can't provide for Noodle!

c11:p60.text:
By and by the beadle comes out, once more intensifying the sensation,
which has rather languished in the interval. He is understood to be
in want of witnesses for the inquest to-morrow who can tell the
coroner and jury anything whatever respecting the deceased. Is
immediately referred to innumerable people who can tell nothing
whatever. Is made more imbecile by being constantly informed that
Mrs. Green’s son “was a law-writer his-self and knowed him better
than anybody,” which son of Mrs. Green’s appears, on inquiry, to be
at the present time aboard a vessel bound for China, three months
out, but considered accessible by telegraph on application to the
Lords of the Admiralty. Beadle goes into various shops and parlours,
examining the inhabitants, always shutting the door first, and by
exclusion, delay, and general idiotcy exasperating the public.
Policeman seen to smile to potboy. Public loses interest and
undergoes reaction. Taunts the beadle in shrill youthful voices with
having boiled a boy, choruses fragments of a popular song to that
effect and importing that the boy was made into soup for the
workhouse. Policeman at last finds it necessary to support the law
and seize a vocalist, who is released upon the flight of the rest on
condition of his getting out of this then, come, and cutting it—a
condition he immediately observes. So the sensation dies off for the
time; and the unmoved policeman (to whom a little opium, more or
less, is nothing), with his shining hat, stiff stock, inflexible
great-coat, stout belt and bracelet, and all things fitting, pursues
his lounging way with a heavy tread, beating the palms of his white
gloves one against the other and stopping now and then at a
street-corner to look casually about for anything between a lost
child and a murder.
c11:p60.summary: The beadle ineffectually seeks inquest witnesses; the public mocks and taunts him while the policeman maintains indifferent order.
c11:p60.best_quote: the public immediately refers to innumerable people who can tell nothing whatever

c25:p58.text:
A ghostly shade, frilled and night-capped, follows the law-stationer

For the watchful Mrs. Snagsby is there too—bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow.

c17:p52.text:
“My dear Mother Hubbard,” he said, “that’s the very thing! I have
thought of that several times and have been quite angry with myself
for meaning to be so much in earnest and—somehow—not exactly being

c17:p51.text:
But even Ada, with her loving face—and if it had seemed innocent and
trusting when I first saw it in that memorable November fog, how much
more did it seem now when I knew her innocent and trusting
heart—even Ada shook her head at this and looked serious. So I
thought it a good opportunity to hint to Richard that if he were
sometimes a little careless of himself, I was very sure he never
